failure_modes.description: Controllers can evaluate multiple strategies simultaneously
failure_modes.evidence: Real-world traffic controllers have limited processing capacity and cannot practically evaluate multiple complex timing strategies in real-time while also managing actual traffic flow.

failure_modes.description: Evolutionary process leads to global optimization
failure_modes.evidence: Evolutionary algorithms are well-known to often converge to local optima rather than global optima, especially in complex, multi-modal optimization problems like traffic flow.

failure_modes.description: Network can inherit and combine beneficial strategies
failure_modes.evidence: Traffic systems exist in heterogeneous environments with different intersection geometries, traffic patterns, and regulatory constraints that prevent straightforward inheritance and combination of strategies.
Numerous prior studies have applied evolutionary algorithms to traffic signal optimization, with limited success due to the computational complexity and real-time constraints of the problem.

failure_modes.description: Inability to adapt to changing traffic patterns
failure_modes.evidence: The hypothesis explicitly lists this as an expected failure mode, indicating the proponents acknowledge the system cannot handle dynamic changes - a critical flaw for a traffic control system.

failure_modes.description: Traffic signal optimization as evolutionary process
failure_modes.evidence: Traffic systems require deterministic, predictable behavior for safety and efficiency, while evolutionary processes are inherently probabilistic and may produce unpredictable or unsafe timing configurations.
